headline: High: OpenHands can read/write mounted files and use MCP while kotaemon handles API keys and broad network egress, creating default data-leak and action-conflict risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can use MCP and read/write runtime files, so attacker-controlled content in shared files or tool outputs could be treated as instructions. Kotaemon processes documents/HTML/PDFs and exposes a web UI, making it plausible that its outputs are copied into OpenHands. The pair lacks a documented provenance barrier, so injection is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF kotaemon outputs are copied into OpenHands without provenance tagging, prompt injection is possible.
IF both agents share a mounted workspace or MCP channel, attacker-controlled content can bridge them.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of kotaemon outputs into OpenHands.
Use a read-only handoff folder for any shared artifacts.
Add provenance labels to all transferred documents.
Restrict MCP servers to allowlisted, trusted endpoints.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping before handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Kotaemon touches API keys and broad document classes, while OpenHands reads files in its runtime sandbox and can write them back out with broad network egress. If they share mounted files or a workspace, sensitive documents or secrets can flow from kotaemon into OpenHands and then to external model providers or MCP servers. That creates a default exfiltration path.
conditions: IF kotaemon stores secrets or sensitive documents in ./ktem_app_data and OpenHands mounts that path, leakage is possible.
IF OpenHands sends runtime file contents to a configured model provider or MCP server, data can leave the pair.
mitigations: Keep kotaemon data and OpenHands runtime on separate volumes.
Remove secrets from any shared directory before launch.
Disable outbound network for OpenHands except approved endpoints.
Use per-agent credentials instead of shared API keys.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP or secret-scanning on shared mounts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; kotaemon also supports multiple instances and uses a shared app-data directory. If both are pointed at the same workspace, concurrent writes can corrupt files or git state. The profiles do not show locking or coordination, so the conflict risk is material in default multi-agent use.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same mounted directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF OpenHands modifies git state in a repo that kotaemon also reads or writes, race conditions are possible.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories to each agent.
Freeze git operations to one agent at a time.
Use file locks for any shared artifacts.
Make kotaemon outputs read-only before OpenHands consumes them.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level coordination/locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Kotaemon produces document-grounded answers and citations, and OpenHands can act on inputs with shell, browser, and git tools. If OpenHands treats kotaemon output as authoritative, a mistaken or injected answer can cascade into code changes, emails, or other actions. The pair has no documented verification step, but the blast radius is not guaranteed to be irreversible.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses kotaemon answers as ground truth without verification, errors can cascade.
IF OpenHands is allowed to take downstream actions based on kotaemon citations, the impact expands beyond a single response.
mitigations: Require human review before any action-taking step.
Cross-check kotaemon outputs against source documents.
Limit OpenHands to draft-only mode for tasks sourced from kotaemon.
Mark kotaemon outputs as untrusted until verified.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Kotaemon explicitly handles API keys and chat transcripts, while OpenHands runs model-provider calls and stores files in a runtime sandbox. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into kotaemon and then moved into OpenHands, retention and residency controls may diverge across the two systems. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so the safest reading is a policy mismatch risk.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed in kotaemon and then copied into OpenHands, retention obligations may diverge.
IF the two agents are deployed in different regions or under different logging policies, compliance gaps can arise.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces.
Align retention settings before exchanging artifacts.
Document which agent is the system of record for each data class.
Purge sensitive runtime files after each task.
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls across both agents.
